summary.text: Explicit finite witness tables supply Goldbach decompositions through 8012 and Lemoine decompositions through 15727, while above those bounds positivity directly yields the corresponding prime decomposition. For any bound, applying the even case to a sufficiently large integer produces cousin-prime pairs \((q,q+6)\) and \((p-6,p)\), and the size of their sum forces at least one lower member to exceed the bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(n)=\frac{3-(-1)^n}{2}.
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. By the definition of A219055, \(a(n)>0\) means that there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
 n=p+c(n)q,\qquad p>q,
\]
and, in addition, \(p-6\) and \(q+6\) are prime. Equivalently, one may choose \(q<n\), put
\[
 p=n-c(n)q,
\]
and require
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,
\]
\[
 q,\ q+6,\ n-c(n)q,\ n-c(n)q-6\quad\text{all prime}.
\]
Indeed, \((c(n)+1)q<n\) is exactly \(q<n-c(n)q=p\).

Assume throughout the core conjecture:

* if \(n>8012\) is even, then \(a(n)>0\);
* if \(n>15727\) is odd, then \(a(n)>0\).

We prove the three asserted consequences.

First we record the two finite facts needed below.

**Finite representation facts.**

1. Every even integer \(m\) with \(4\le m\le8012\) is a sum of two primes.
2. Every odd integer \(m\) with \(7\le m\le15727\) has the form \(m=p+2q\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are prime.

Here is the finite computation establishing these facts and how it is organized. For each relevant \(m\), one searches through \(q=2,3,4,\ldots,m\). In the first computation one retains a \(q\) for which both \(q\) and \(m-q\) are prime. In the second one retains a \(q\) for which both \(q\) and \(m-2q\) are prime. Each claimed prime is checked by trial division by every integer, or equivalently every prime, not exceeding its square root. Thus every retained entry directly gives the displayed representation; no probabilistic primality test is involved.

For bookkeeping, the Goldbach search is divided into the arithmetic progressions of even numbers beginning at
\[
4,804,1604,2404,3204,4004,4804,5604,6404,7204,8004.
\]
For each of the first ten starting values \(s\), the computation supplies one witness \(q_k\) for each number
\[
 m=s+2k\qquad(0\le k<400),
\]
checking that \(q_k\) and \(s+2k-q_k\) are prime. These blocks cover the even numbers from \(4\) through \(8002\). The last block supplies witnesses for
\[
8004,8006,8008,8010,8012.
\]
For example, the initial witnesses give
\[
4=2+2,\quad6=3+3,\quad8=3+5,\quad10=3+7,
\]
and the same direct prime-pair check is made for every subsequent entry in the indicated finite progressions. This proves finite fact 1.

Similarly, the Lemoine search is divided into the progressions of odd numbers beginning at
\[
\begin{split}
&7,807,1607,2407,3207,4007,4807,5607,6407,7207,\\
&8007,8807,9607,10407,11207,12007,12807,13607,14407,15207.
\end{split}
\]
For each of the first nineteen starting values \(s\), a witness \(q_k\) is supplied for each
\[
 m=s+2k\qquad(0\le k<400),
\]
and the two numbers \(q_k\) and \(s+2k-2q_k\) are checked to be prime. These blocks cover all odd integers from \(7\) through \(15205\). In the final block the same check is made for \(m=15207+2k\) through \(15727\), namely for \(0\le k\le260\). The first few entries, for instance, give
\[
7=3+2\cdot2,\quad9=3+2\cdot3,\quad11=5+2\cdot3,
\]
and all remaining entries are checked in exactly the same finite way. This proves finite fact 2.

The block description also explains why there are no omissions. An even \(m\) in the first range has a unique expression \(m=s+2k\) in one of the listed even blocks, and an odd \(m\) in the second range has a unique such expression in one of the listed odd blocks. In each case the retained entry at position \(k\) gives the required two primes.

We now turn to the consequences of the core conjecture.

### 1. Goldbach's conjecture

Let \(n\ge4\) be even. We must express \(n\) as a sum of two primes.

If \(n\le8012\), finite fact 1 gives primes \(p,q\) with
\[
n=p+q.
\]

Suppose instead that \(n>8012\). The core conjecture says that \(a(n)>0\). Since \(n\) is even, \(c(n)=1\). Hence positivity of \(a(n)\) supplies primes \(p,q\) satisfying
\[
n=p+q.
\]
(The additional conclusions that \(p>q\), \(p-6\) is prime, and \(q+6\) is prime are not needed here.) Thus every even \(n\ge4\) is a sum of two primes, which is Goldbach's conjecture in the stated form.

### 2. Lemoine's conjecture

Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. We must express \(n\) as \(p+2q\) with \(p,q\) prime.

If \(n\le15727\), this follows from finite fact 2.

If \(n>15727\), the core conjecture gives \(a(n)>0\). Now \(n\) is odd, so \(c(n)=2\). Consequently there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
n=p+2q.
\]
Again the further prime conditions in the definition of A219055 are stronger than what is needed. This proves Lemoine's conjecture.

### 3. Infinitely many cousin-prime pairs

It remains to prove that the set
\[
\mathcal C=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ and }r+6\text{ are prime}\}
\]
is infinite. It is enough to prove that \(\mathcal C\) is unbounded: a finite set of natural numbers has a largest element, so a member above every prescribed bound rules out finiteness.

Fix an arbitrary natural number \(B\). Set
\[
n=2(B+8014)=2B+16028.
\]
Then \(n\) is even and certainly \(n>8012\). The core conjecture therefore gives a representation counted by \(a(n)\). Since \(n\) is even, there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
n=p+q,
\]
with
\[
p>q,
\]
and such that
\[
p-6\quad\text{and}\quad q+6
\]
are also prime. In particular, both
\[
(q,q+6)\quad\text{and}\quad(p-6,p)
\]
are cousin-prime pairs. We show that at least one of their lower members exceeds \(B\).

There are two cases.

If \(q>B\), then \(q\in\mathcal C\) because both \(q\) and \(q+6\) are prime, and it already lies above the prescribed bound.

Otherwise \(q\le B\). Put
\[
r=p-6=n-q-6.
\]
Both \(r=p-6\) and \(r+6=p\) are prime, so \(r\in\mathcal C\). Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
r
 &=2(B+8014)-q-6\\
 &\ge 2(B+8014)-B-6\\
 &=B+16022\\
 &>B.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus this second cousin-prime pair has lower member greater than \(B\).

In either case there is an \(r>B\) for which both \(r\) and \(r+6\) are prime. Since \(B\) was arbitrary, \(\mathcal C\) is unbounded and hence infinite.

We have therefore derived Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs differing by \(6\) from the assumed positivity of A219055 above the two stated parity-dependent thresholds.
